content: Aspergum, known generically as Aspirin Gum-Oral, is the United States trademark name for a chewing gum that contains aspirin as its active ingredient. This acetylsalicylic acid-based gum typically delivers a dose of 227 mg (equivalent to 3 ½ grains) of aspirin and is available in cherry and orange flavors. The aspirin in this gum provides therapeutic effects, including analgesic, salicylate, anti-inflammatory, and antipyretic properties, making it useful for managing pain, arthritis, and fever. The trademark for Aspergum is currently owned by Insight Pharmaceuticals, the same company that manufactures Anacin, a product combining aspirin and caffeine. Medicated chewing gum containing aspirin was first introduced in the United States in 1924. In December 1927, Frank M. Dillard, the inventor of Feenamint, and William C.S. obtained trademark protection for Aspergum. By 1928, Dillard-Nalle began selling Dillard's Aspergum in the United States. This product was an early example of functional gum, serving as a drug delivery system. It played a significant role in recognizing aspirin's antithrombotic effects. In 1953, general practitioner Dr. Lawrence Craven observed that patients who chewed Aspergum as an analgesic after tonsillectomy experienced increased bleeding tendencies. This discovery led to the widespread use of low-dose aspirin by physicians to prevent heart attacks and strokes. Emergency rooms also began routinely administering aspirin to patients suspected of experiencing a heart attack. In June 1993, Farmades Spa, based in Rome, Italy, started manufacturing Aspergum Confetti Gommosi Masticabili for sale in Italy. Over time, people have found unique uses for the gum. For instance, in her 1997 book Streisand, Academy Award-winning singer Barbra Streisand recounted how she used Aspergum to fill the gap left by the removal of two front teeth when she began her career. In 1998, Gumtech announced its plans to produce Aspergum for Schering-Plough HealthCare Products.
